voiceover: Did the apostle Paul believe Jesus existed before he was born? Most stories about Jesus run one way — upward: a teacher so revered that, over time, his followers lifted him higher until they called him God. The striking thing about Paul, our earliest Christian writer, is that his story runs the other way. His Christ is sent from the Father — “God sent forth his Son, born of woman.” The sending is named before the birth. “Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor.” You can't become poor for someone's sake unless you were rich first. He was “in the form of God” before he was “born in the likeness of men.” He is the one “through whom” the world was made — the agent of creation stands before and outside it. Paul never sets out to prove Christ preexisted; he assumes it, pressed into letter after letter. That is not the language of a man slowly promoted to heaven. It is the language of a descent — a Christ who was already himself before Bethlehem. This is preexistence — a step toward the deity of Christ.

scenes.vo: Did the apostle Paul believe Jesus existed before he was born?
Most stories about Jesus run one way — upward: a teacher so revered that, over time, his followers lifted him higher until they called him God.
The striking thing about Paul, our earliest Christian writer, is that his story runs the other way.
His Christ is sent from the Father — “God sent forth his Son, born of woman.” The sending is named before the birth.
“Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor.” You can't become poor for someone's sake unless you were rich first.
He was “in the form of God” before he was “born in the likeness of men.”
He is the one “through whom” the world was made — the agent of creation stands before and outside it.
Paul never sets out to prove Christ preexisted; he assumes it, pressed into letter after letter.

That is not the language of a man slowly promoted to heaven. It is the language of a descent — a Christ who was already himself before Bethlehem. This is preexistence — a step toward the deity of Christ.

sub.t: A Christ who was already himself
